modern_osis:
Joshua — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan, conquered the land and divided it among the tribes under Joshua's leadership.

It also records the people's history until Joshua's death.

The book wonderfully reveals God's power and faithfulness in fulfilling his promises to Israel.

It also describes his carrying out the judgments he had justly threatened against the Canaanites.

These events should teach us to take seriously the fearful warnings God's word gives to sinners who refuse to repent.

They should also encourage us to seek refuge in Jesus Christ.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Lord appoints Joshua to succeed Moses.1–4God promises to assist Joshua.5–9Preparation to pass over Jordan.10–15The people promise to obey Joshua.16–18
The Lord appoints Joshua (verses 1–4)

Joshua had served Moses faithfully for years.

The person now called to honor had first spent a long time working and learning.

Our Lord Jesus took the form of a servant.

Joshua had learned to obey before receiving authority.

Those who have learned to obey are best fitted to lead.

When useful servants of God are taken away, those who remain should become more diligent in doing good.

God ordered Joshua to rise and cross the Jordan.

At that time the river had overflowed its banks.

Joshua had no boats or bridge.

Yet, because God commanded the crossing, he had to trust that God would open the way.

The promise of God's presence (verses 5–9)

Joshua was to make God's law his rule.

He was commanded to meditate on it day and night so that he would understand it.

No amount of worldly business should cause us to neglect the one thing that is truly necessary.

Everything Joshua commanded the people and every judgment he gave had to agree with God's law.

He remained under that law himself.

No position of power or honor places anyone above God's commands.

Joshua was to draw courage from the promise of God's presence.

His personal weaknesses were no reason to despair.

The all-sufficient God had called, appointed and commissioned him and would uphold him in his duty.

When we are acting according to God's command, we have good reason to be strong and courageous.

Jesus Christ, whom Joshua pictured, was also strengthened through his suffering by his dedication to his Father's will and command.

Israel prepares to cross (verses 10–15)

Joshua told Israel that the people would cross the Jordan and possess Canaan because God had promised it.

We honor God's truth when we do not waver in unbelief concerning his promises.

The two and a half tribes who had settled east of the Jordan had to cross with their brothers.

When God gives us rest, we should consider how we can help others still struggling to obtain it.

The people promise obedience (verses 16–18)

Israel promised Joshua willing obedience.

The people would follow his commands without grumbling or arguing and go wherever he sent them.

The best thing we can ask God to give our civil leaders is his own presence.

That will make them a blessing to the people they serve.

When we pray for them in this way, we also seek our own good.

May we willingly follow the Captain of our salvation, obey his commands and fight the good fight of faith alongside everyone who trusts and loves his name.

Christ's authority will finally prevail.
classic_reading:
[Josh.1.1-Josh.1.4]
Joshua
Here is the history of Israel's passing into the land of Canaan, conquering and dividing it, under the command of Joshua, and their history until his death. The power and truth of God in fulfilling his promises to Israel, and in executing his justly threatened vengeance on the Canaanites, are wonderfully displayed. This should teach us to regard the tremendous curses denounced in the word of God against impenitent sinners, and to seek refuge in Christ Jesus.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The Lord appoints Joshua to succeed Moses. | (1-4) |
God promises to assist Joshua. | (5-9) |
Preparation to pass over Jordan. | (10-15) |
The people promise to obey Joshua. | (16-18) |
Verses 1-4
Joshua had attended upon Moses. He who was called to honour, had been long used to business. Our Lord Jesus took upon him the form of a servant. Joshua was trained up under command. Those are fittest to rule, who have learned to obey. The removal of useful men should quicken survivors to be the more diligent in doing good. Arise, go over Jordan. At this place and at this time the banks were overflowed. Joshua had no bridge or boats, and yet he must believe that God, having ordered the people over, would open a way.
[Josh.1.5-Josh.1.9]
Verses 5-9
Joshua is to make the law of God his rule. He is charged to meditate therein day and night, that he might understand it. Whatever affairs of this world we have to mind, we must not neglect the one thing needful. All his orders to the people, and his judgments, must be according to the law of God. Joshua must himself be under command; no man's dignity or dominion sets him above the law of God. He is to encourage himself with the promise and presence of God. Let not the sense of thine own infirmities dishearten thee; God is all-sufficient. I have commanded, called, and commissioned thee to do it, and will be sure to bear thee out in it. When we are in the way of duty, we have reason to be strong and very bold. Our Lord Jesus, as Joshua here, was borne up under his sufferings by a regard to the will of God, and the commandment from his Father.
[Josh.1.10-Josh.1.15]
Verses 10-15
Joshua says to the people, Ye shall pass over Jordan, and shall possess the land; because God had said so to him. We honour the truth of God, when we stagger not at the promise of God. The two tribes and a half were to go over Jordan with their brethren. When God, by his providence, has given us rest, we ought to consider what service we may do to our brethren.
[Josh.1.16-Josh.1.18]
Verses 16-18
The people of Israel engage to obey Joshua; All that thou commandest us to do we will readily do, without murmuring or disputing, and whithersoever thou sendest us we will go. The best we can ask of God for our magistrates, is, that they may have the presence of God; that will make them blessings to us, so that in seeking this for them, we consult our own interest. May we be enabled to enlist under the banner of the Captain of our salvation, to be obedient to his commands, and to fight the good fight of faith, with all that trust in and love his name, against all who oppose his authority; for whoever refuses to obey him must be destroyed.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesRahab receives and hides two Israelites.1–7Rahab and the spies.8–21The return of the spies.22–24
Rahab protects the spies (verses 1–7)

Faith in God's promises does not make careful action unnecessary.

Instead, faith encourages us to use the appropriate means.

God's providence guided Israel's spies to Rahab's home.

God knew there was someone there who would be faithful to them, although they could not have known it.

Rahab appears to have been an innkeeper.

Henry thinks her former reputation for immoral living is uncertain; if it was true, she had left those practices behind.

Events that appear accidental to us often serve great purposes under God's providence.

Rahab welcomed the spies despite her king and nation's hostility to Israel.

Her action was an expression of faith (James 2:25).

True faith gave her courage to rise above fear of other people and cast in her lot with God's people.

She helped them because she respected Israel and its God, not because she expected profit or intended wrongdoing.

But Henry refuses to excuse the falsehood she told.

Even if excuses can be suggested, we should not explain away her guilt.

Her knowledge of God's law was limited.

A similar lie told by someone possessing the fuller light of revelation would deserve serious correction.

Rahab and the spies agree on her protection (verses 8–21)

Rahab had heard of God's miracles for Israel.

She trusted that his promises and warnings would certainly come true.

She recognized that safety lay only in submitting to him and joining his people.

This revealed the genuine principle of divine faith within her.

Notice the spies' promises.

God's goodness is described through kindness and truth (Psalm 117:2).

We should imitate him in both qualities.

People who intend to keep promises conscientiously will make them carefully.

The spies included necessary conditions in their agreement.

The scarlet cord recalls the Passover blood placed upon Israelite doorposts.

It pictured the sinner's safety under Christ's atoning blood and the need to seek refuge there from God's righteous judgment.

The cord Rahab used to help save the spies would also be used for her own safety.

What we employ in honoring and serving God may become an instrument of his blessing toward us.

The spies report to Joshua (verses 22–24)

The spies returned with encouraging news.

The people of Canaan were losing courage because of Israel.

They had neither the wisdom to surrender nor the courage to resist.

A troubled conscience and fear of God's anger may terrify ungodly people without leading them to repentance.

That fear can be a warning that judgment is near.

But even the greatest sinners may still receive abundant grace.

Let them flee without delay to Christ, and all will be well.
classic_reading:
[Josh.2.1-Josh.2.7]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Rahab receives and hides two Israelites. | (1-7) |
Rahab and the spies. | (8-21) |
The return of the spies. | (22-24) |
Verses 1-7
Faith in God's promises ought not to do away, but to encourage our diligence in the use of proper means. The providence of God directed the spies to the house of Rahab. God knew where there was one that would be true to them, though they did not. Rahab appears to have been an innkeeper; and if she had formerly been one of bad life, which is doubtful, she had left her evil courses. That which seems to us most accidental, is often overruled by the Divine providence to serve great ends. It was by faith that Rahab received those with peace, against whom her king and country had war. We are sure this was a good work; it is so spoken of by the apostle, [Jas.2.25] Jas 2:25; and she did it by faith, such a faith as set her above the fear of man. Those only are true believers, who find in their hearts to venture for God; they take his people for their people, and cast in their lot among them. The spies were led by the special providence of God, and Rahab entertained them out of regard to Israel and Israel's God, and not for lucre or for any evil purpose. Though excuses may be offered for the guilt of Rahab's falsehood, it seems best to admit nothing which tends to explain it away. Her views of the Divine law must have been very dim: a falsehood like this, told by those who enjoy the light of revelation, whatever the motive, would deserve heavy censure.
[Josh.2.8-Josh.2.21]
Verses 8-21
Rahab had heard of the miracles the Lord wrought for Israel. She believed that his promises would certainly be fulfilled, and his threatenings take effect; and that there was no way of escape but by submitting to him, and joining with his people. The conduct of Rahab proved that she had the real principle of Divine faith. Observe the promises the spies made to her. The goodness of God is often expressed by his kindness and truth, [Ps.117.2] Psa 117:2; in both these we must be followers of him. Those who will be conscientious in keeping promises, are cautious in making them. The spies make needful conditions. The scarlet cord, like the blood upon the doorpost at the passover, recalls to remembrance the sinner's security under the atoning blood of Christ; and that we are to flee thereto for refuge from the wrath of a justly offended God. The same cord Rahab used for the saving of these Israelites, was to be used for her own safety. What we serve and honour God with, we may expect he will bless, and make useful to us.
[Josh.2.22-Josh.2.24]
Verses 22-24
The report the spies brought was encouraging. All the people of the country faint because of Israel; they have neither wisdom to yield, nor courage to fight. Those terrors of conscience, and that sense of Divine wrath, which dismay the ungodly, but bring not to repentance, are fearful forebodings of approaching destruction. But grace yet abounds to the chief of sinners. Let them, without delay, flee to Christ, and all shall be well.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Israelites come to Jordan.1–6The Lord encourages joshua—Joshua encourages the people.7–13The Israelites pass through Jordan on dry land.14–17
Israel approaches the Jordan (verses 1–6)

The Israelites approached the Jordan in faith.

They had been told they would cross and therefore came as far as they could.

When we know our duty, we should proceed as far as possible and trust the Lord to open the way.

Joshua rose early.

Scripture makes special mention of his early rising here and on other occasions.

He valued doing God's work more than personal ease.

People who accomplish important things must not be ruled by a love of sleep.

Anyone occupying public office should attend faithfully to the duties of that position.

The people were to follow the ark.

Likewise, we must follow God's word and the Holy Spirit's guidance in everything.

We should follow ministers only as far as they follow Christ.

The way across the Jordan was unlike anything Israel had encountered before.

Our lives also bring roads we have never walked and challenges we have never faced.

Yet in the path of duty we can go forward with courage and joy.

Poverty, suffering, exhausting work, persecution, public shame and even death may lie along that road.

But Christ, the Author and Perfecter of our faith, has already traveled it.

By faith we can see his footsteps along every dangerous stretch of the journey.

He invites us to follow him toward the glory where he now is.

Israel had to consecrate itself.

If we wish to experience God's love and power, we must put away sin and avoid grieving the Holy Spirit.

The Lord strengthens Joshua and Israel (verses 7–13)

God announced that the Jordan's waters would be cut off.

This would repeat the wonder of the Red Sea, though in different circumstances.

The Lord has just as much power to finish the salvation of his people as he has to begin it.

God's word was with Joshua as truly as it had been with Moses.

His acts of favor toward his people should strengthen our faith and hope.

The Lord's work is perfect.

He will preserve those who belong to him.

The Jordan's overflowing water could not keep Israel out of Canaan.

And the power of Canaan's inhabitants could not drive Israel out again while God stood with the people.

Israel crosses the river on dry ground (verses 14–17)

The Jordan had overflowed all its banks.

This made the miracle of crossing even more remarkable and displayed God's kindness.

However strong the opposition to God's saving work may become, he can overcome it.

After the long and weary wilderness journey, entering Canaan through the Jordan pictured a believer's passage through death into heaven.

Jesus, pictured by the ark, has gone before his people.

He crossed the river when it was overflowing.

Let us treasure our experiences of his faithful, tender care.

Their memory will strengthen our faith and hope in our final struggle.
classic_reading:
[Josh.3.1-Josh.3.6]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The Israelites come to Jordan. | (1-6) |
The Lord encourages joshua--Joshua encourages the people.
(7-13)
The Israelites pass through Jordan on dry land. | (14-17) |
Verses 1-6
The Israelites came to Jordan in faith, having been told that they should pass it. In the way of duty, let us proceed as far as we can, and depend on the Lord. Joshua led them. Particular notice is taken of his early rising, as afterwards upon other occasions, which shows how little he sought his own ease. Those who would bring great things to pass, must rise early. Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty. All in public stations should always attend to the duty of their place. The people were to follow the ark. Thus must we walk after the rule of the word, and the direction of the Spirit, in everything; so shall peace be upon us as upon the Israel of God; but we must follow our ministers only as they follow Christ. All their way through the wilderness was an untrodden path, but most so this through Jordan. While we are here, we must expect and prepare to pass ways that we have not passed before; but in the path of duty we may proceed with boldness and cheerfulness. Whether we are called to suffer poverty, pain, labour, persecution, reproach, or death, we are following the Author and Finisher of our faith; nor can we set our feet in any dangerous or difficult spot, through our whole journey, but faith will there see the prints of the Redeemer's feet, who trod that very path to glory above, and bids us follow him, that where he is, we may be also. They were to sanctify themselves. Would we experience the effects of God's love and power, we must put away sin, and be careful not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God.
[Josh.3.7-Josh.3.13]
Verses 7-13
The waters of Jordan shall be cut off. This must be done in such a way as never was done, but in the dividing of the Red sea. That miracle is here repeated; God has the same power to finish the salvation of his people, as to begin it; the WORD of the Lord was as truly with Joshua as with Moses. God's appearances for his people ought to encourage faith and hope. God's work is perfect, he will keep his people. Jordan's flood cannot keep out Israel, Canaan's force cannot turn them out again.
[Josh.3.14-Josh.3.17]
Verses 14-17
Jordan overflowed all its banks. This magnified the power of God, and his kindness to Israel. Although those who oppose the salvation of God's people have all advantages, yet God can and will conquer. This passage over Jordan, as an entrance to Canaan, after their long, weary wanderings in the wilderness, shadowed out the believer's passage through death to heaven, after he has finished his wanderings in this sinful world. Jesus, typified by the ark, hath gone before, and he crossed the river when it most flooded the country around. Let us treasure up experiences of His faithful and tender care, that they may help our faith and hope in the last conflict.

Memorial stones taken from the river (verses 1–9)

The Lord's works are so worthy of remembrance, and human hearts so prone to forget them, that we need frequent reminders.

Such reminders honor God.

They benefit us and our children.

God therefore commanded Israel to prepare a memorial of the Jordan crossing.

The crossing is completed (verses 10–19)

The priests carrying the ark did not move until the Lord directed them.

No one should grow weary of waiting while the signs of God's presence remain with them, even in the depths of hardship.

God also honored Joshua.

People are respected in the best way and for the best reason when others recognize that the Lord is with them and that they live before him.

The memorial at Gilgal (verses 20–24)

Parents should teach their children about God's words and works from an early age, training them to follow his ways.

In everything we teach children, we should lead them to fear and honor the Lord.

Sincere faith is the best education.

We are just as obligated as Israel to praise our God's kindness.

Should we not establish memorials of gratitude toward the Lord, who has brought us through danger and distress in so many remarkable ways?

He has helped us just as truly as he helped the faithful people of earlier generations.

How ungrateful and unthinking we are when we fail to recognize his hand in our repeated deliverances!

[Josh.4.1-Josh.4.9]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Stones taken out of Jordan. | (1-9) |
The people pass through Jordan. | (10-19) |
The twelve stones placed in Gilgal. | (20-24) |
Verses 1-9
The works of the Lord are so worthy of rememberance, and the heart of man is so prone to forget them, that various methods are needful to refresh our memories, for the glory of God, our advantage, and that of our children. God gave orders for preparing this memorial.
[Josh.4.10-Josh.4.19]
Verses 10-19
The priests with the ark did not stir till ordered to move. Let none be weary of waiting, while they have the tokens of God's presence with them, even the ark of the covenant, though it be in the depths of adversity. Notice is taken of the honour put upon Joshua. Those are feared in the best manner, and to the best purpose, who make it appear that God is with them, and that they set him before them.
[Josh.4.20-Josh.4.24]
Verses 20-24
It is the duty of parents to tell their children betimes of the words and works of God, that they may be trained up in the way they should go. In all the instruction parents give their children, they should teach them to fear God. Serious godliness is the best learning. Are we not called, as much as the Israelites, to praise the loving-kindness of our God? Shall we not raise a pillar to our God, who has brought us through dangers and distresses in so wonderful a way? For hitherto the Lord hath helped us, as much as he did his saints of old. How great the stupidity and ingratitude of men, who perceive not His hand, and will not acknowledge his goodness, in their frequent deliverances!

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Canaanites are afraid, Circumcision renewed.1–9The passover at Gilgal, The manna ceases.10–12The Captain of the Lord's host appears to Joshua.13–15
Circumcision is renewed at Gilgal (verses 1–9)

How dreadful is the condition of people who see God's righteous judgment approaching but cannot turn it away or escape it!

That will be the final condition of the wicked.

The anguish and fear cannot adequately be described.

If only sinners would heed the warning now, before it is too late, and flee to the refuge offered in the gospel!

God brought such fear upon the Canaanites, breaking their courage.

This gave Israel a brief period of rest.

Circumcision was renewed and the disgrace associated with Egypt was rolled away.

The people were publicly acknowledged as God's freeborn children, bearing the seal of his covenant.

When God completes his people's salvation, he silences their enemies and turns their reproaches back upon them.

Passover is observed and manna ceases (verses 10–12)

Israel celebrated the Passover at its appointed time on the plains near Jericho, despite the hostile Canaanites nearby.

The Lord fulfilled his promise that, when the people gathered for the appointed feasts, their land would remain under his special protection (Exodus 34:24).

Manna ceased as soon as the Israelites ate the old grain of Canaan.

God had provided it when they needed it.

He kept providing it for precisely as long as it was necessary.

We should not expect miraculous provision when the same needs can be met through ordinary means.

God's word and appointed acts of worship are like spiritual manna, feeding his people through the wilderness of this world.

Although we repeatedly forfeit these gifts through our sin, he graciously continues giving them while we remain here.

When we enter heavenly Canaan, we will no longer need them in the same way.

Joshua meets the Captain of the Lord's army (verses 13–15)

This is the first recorded appearance of God's glory to Joshua.

Someone appeared before him in the form of a man.

Henry identifies him as the Son of God, the eternal Word.

Joshua gave the visitor divine honor.

He received that honor, which a merely created angel would refuse.

He is also called Jehovah in Joshua 6:2.

Christ appeared to Abraham as a traveler and to Joshua as a warrior.

He meets his people in the way their faith and circumstances require.

The Captain held a drawn sword.

This encouraged Joshua to prosecute the war courageously.

It showed that Christ was ready to defend and rescue his people.

Joshua needed to know whether this person was a friend or enemy.

In the conflict between Christ and Satan, no one can remain neutral as they might in ordinary disputes.

Joshua's question showed his genuine desire to know and obey the Lord's will.

Every true Christian must fight under Christ's banner.

Through his presence and help, they will overcome.
classic_reading:
[Josh.5.1-Josh.5.9]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
The Canaanites are afraid, Circumcision renewed. | (1-9) |
The passover at Gilgal, The manna ceases. | (10-12) |
The Captain of the Lord's host appears to Joshua. | (13-15) |
Verses 1-9
How dreadful is their case, who see the wrath of God advancing towards them, without being able to turn it aside, or escape it! Such will be the horrible situation of the wicked; nor can words express the anguish of their feelings, or the greatness of their terror. Oh that they would now take warning, and before it be too late, flee for refuge to lay hold upon that hope set before them in the gospel! God impressed these fears on the Canaanites, and dispirited them. This gave a short rest to the Israelites, and circumcision rolled away the reproach of Egypt. They were hereby owned to be the free-born children of God, having the seal of the covenant. When God glorifies himself in perfecting the salvation of his people, he not only silences all enemies, but rolls back their reproaches upon themselves.
[Josh.5.10-Josh.5.12]
Verses 10-12
A solemn passover was kept, at the time appointed by the law, in the plains of Jericho, in defiance of the Canaanites round about them. It was a performance of the promise, that when they went up to keep the feasts, their land should be under the special protection of the Divine providence, [Exod.34.24] Ex 34:24. Notice is taken of the ceasing of the manna as soon as they had eaten the old corn of the land. For as it came just when they needed, so it continued as long as they needed it. This teaches us not to expect supplies by miracles, when they may be had in a common way. The word and ordinances of God are spiritual manna, with which God nourishes his people in this wilderness. Though often forfeited, yet they are continued while we are here; but when we come to the heavenly Canaan, this manna will cease, for we shall no longer need it.
[Josh.5.13-Josh.5.15]
Verses 13-15
We read not of any appearance of God's glory to Joshua till now. There appeared to him one as a man to be noticed. This Man was the Son of God, the eternal Word. Joshua gave him Divine honours: he received them, which a created angel would not have done, and he is called Jehovah, chap. 6:2. To Abraham he appeared as a traveller; to Joshua as a man of war. Christ will be to his people what their faith needs. Christ had his sword drawn, which encouraged Joshua to carry on the war with vigour. Christ's sword drawn in his hand, denotes how ready he is for the defence and salvation of his people. His sword turns every way. Joshua will know whether he is a friend or a foe. The cause between the Israelites and Canaanites, between Christ and Beelzebub, will not admit of any man's refusing to take one part or the other, as he may do in worldly contests. Joshua's inquiry shows an earnest desire to know the will of Christ, and a cheerful readiness and resolution to do it. All true Christians must fight under Christ's banner, and they will conquer by his presence and assistance.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe siege of Jericho.1–5The city is compassed.6–16Jericho is taken, Rahab and her family are saved.17–27
The siege of Jericho (verses 1–5)

Jericho was determined not to submit to Israel. The city was strongly fortified, both by its position and by human defenses, and its gates were shut.

But the people were foolishly strengthening themselves against the Almighty. Their hardened hearts would bring about their destruction.

God had determined that Israel would take Jericho, and quickly. The people were not commanded to prepare an ordinary military siege.

By this unusual method, the Lord honored the ark as the visible sign of his presence. He taught Israel that every victory would come from him.

The people's faith and patience were tested and strengthened.

Israel marches around the city (verses 6–16)

Wherever the ark went, the people followed.

Likewise, ministers should sound the trumpet of the everlasting gospel, proclaiming freedom and victory and encouraging Christians in their spiritual conflict.

God's promised deliverances must be sought in his way and awaited at his time.

At last, when the command came, the people shouted, and Jericho's walls fell.

This was a shout of faith: they believed God's promise that the walls would fall.

It was also a shout of prayer: they cried to heaven for help, and help came.

Jericho falls, and Rahab's family is spared (verses 17–27)

Jericho became a solemn and dreadful offering to God's justice against a people who had filled up the measure of their sins.

The One who had given the inhabitants life as their Creator now carried out the sentence their sins had deserved.

Rahab was not destroyed with those who did not believe (Hebrews 11:31).

Her relatives were spared with her. In this Henry sees a picture of the salvation that comes to a household through faith in Christ (Acts 16:31).

They were rescued like burning pieces of wood snatched from the fire.

The choice before us is equally serious: will we belong to Rahab's company or to the people of Jericho?

Our portion depends on whether we receive or reject the sign of salvation—faith in Christ working through love.

Let us remember the weight of that choice and act accordingly.

Where God's curse rests, no one can escape its consequences. It brings ruin beyond remedy.

Chapter Outline
The siege of Jericho. | (1-5) |
The city is compassed. | (6-16) |
Jericho is taken, Rahab and her family are saved. | (17-27) |
Verses 1-5
Jericho resolves Israel shall not be its master. It shut itself up, being strongly fortified both by art and nature. Thus were they foolish, and their hearts hardened to their destruction; the miserable case of all that strengthen themselves against the Almighty. God resolves Israel shall be its master, and that quickly. No warlike preparations were to be made. By the uncommon method of besieging the city, the Lord honoured the ark, as the symbol of his presence, and showed that all the victories were from him. The faith and patience of the people were proved and increased.
[Josh.6.6-Josh.6.16]
Verses 6-16
Wherever the ark went, the people attended it. God's ministers, by the trumpet of the everlasting gospel, which proclaims liberty and victory, must encourage the followers of Christ in their spiritual warfare. As promised deliverances must be expected in God's way, so they must be expected in his time. At last the people were to shout: they did so, and the walls fell. This was a shout of faith; they believed the walls of Jericho would fall. It was a shout of prayer; they cry to Heaven for help, and help came.
[Josh.6.17-Josh.6.27]
Verses 17-27
Jericho was to be a solemn and awful sacrifice to the justice of God, upon those who had filled up the measure of their sins. So He appoints, from whom, as creatures, they received their lives, and to whom, as sinners, they had forfeited them. Rahab perished not with them that believed not, [Heb.11.31] He 11:31. All her kindred were saved with her; thus faith in Christ brings salvation to the house, [Acts.16.31] Ac 16:31. She, and they with her, were plucked as brands from the burning. With Rahab, or with the men of Jericho; our portion must be assigned, as we posses or disregard the sign of salvation; even faith in Christ, which worketh by love. Let us remember what depends upon our choice, and let us choose accordingly.
